t: Introduction: pathomorphology of COPD and lecture plan
n: In this lesson we study the pathomorphology of COPD. COPD, that is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, is a general umbrella term for lung diseases that progressively worsen airflow. Emphysema is one of the commonest components of COPD: in it the elasticity of the lung is lost and gas exchange is impaired. The second part is devoted to the small airways. Cartilage-free bronchioles with a diameter of less than 2 mm are heavily affected already in the earliest stages of COPD. Aim: to understand the changes of emphysema and small airways and their early detection, and to master the principle of early detection, early diagnosis and early intervention.

t: COPD and emphysema: definition, morphology, signs
n: Emphysema is a progressive enlargement of the air spaces distal to the terminal bronchioles, resulting from destruction of the walls of these spaces. The air sacs rupture in time, forming one large sac, and air is trapped. Oxygen passes into the blood with difficulty, and the lungs become increasingly overfilled. Signs: breathlessness, chronic cough with sputum, wheezing and tightness in the chest. At first they may be mild and go unnoticed. The disease occurs in about 9–10 per cent of the world's population and is expected in the coming years to occupy third place among causes of death.

We consider the risk factors for emphysema. The main risk factor is cigarette smoking. Environmental factors are also important: air pollution, dust and chemicals. In air pollution, the secondary organic aerosols, SOA, in the composition of particles have been cited as an important risk factor for the development of emphysema. The genetic factor is alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. Alpha-1 antitrypsin is the main physiological inhibitor of neutrophil elastase, and its deficiency raises the risk especially in smokers. Repeated respiratory infections, for example pneumonia, and asthma also raise the risk of emphysema or accelerate its development.

Let us take a general look at the hypotheses of pathogenesis. The pathogenesis of emphysema is complex and not fully understood. The alveoli are mainly damaged, and the small airways indirectly. The protease–antiprotease imbalance is regarded as the central hypothesis in genetic and smoking-related emphysema. In it, elastin is broken down. The oxidant–antioxidant imbalance enhances protease and increases apoptosis. In the inflammatory and immune response, macrophages, CD8+ T cells and the elastokine cycle take part. Attention: damage to elastic fibres and loss of tissue traction are a consequence. They cannot be regarded as the primary cause.

We look at the chain of the protease–antiprotease imbalance. Under the action of long-term smoking and other factors a protease-rich environment is created. Proteases mainly break down elastin. Deficiency of alpha-1 antitrypsin, A1AT, the inhibitor of neutrophil elastase, NE, predisposes to emphysema. Thus protease predominates, the inhibitor is scarce, elastin is broken down, structure is lost and emphysema arises. Experiment confirms this idea: if the protease gene is deleted, the mouse is protected, and if protease is introduced into the lung, emphysema appears.

Now the oxidant–antioxidant imbalance. Oxidants, that is hydrogen peroxide, nitric oxide and others, damage proteins, lipids and nucleic acids. Oxidants inactivate protease inhibitors, and newly recruited cells intensify the cycle. The cycle is as follows: smoking and pollution, release of oxidants and cytokines, arrival of neutrophils and macrophages, inactivation of inhibitors, then proteolysis and cell death. Nrf2, that is erythroid-2-related factor, regulates the synthesis of catalase and glutathione. If it is impaired, emphysema worsens.

Inflammation forms a self-sustaining loop. Irritants such as smoking release cytokines, oxidants and proteases, damaging the alveolar wall. Fragments of elastin, that is elastokines, have chemotactic and pro-inflammatory properties. As a result, new cells are recruited and the loop begins again. Neutralising elastokines or blocking their binding to their receptor is considered as a theoretical therapeutic target.

We consider the persistent immune response and apoptosis. In bronchoalveolar lavage fluid and in tissue analysis, regardless of disease severity, macrophages predominate. In these macrophages phagocytosis is somewhat impaired, and they release molecules that damage tissue. CD8+ lymphocytes also contribute to pathogenesis. The cellular inflammatory response appears to continue even after smoking has stopped. In emphysematous lung tissue, the number of apoptotic epithelial and endothelial cells in the alveolar septa is increased. The same was found in experimental animals.

t: Elastic fibre damage and disturbance of mechanical forces
n: Elastic fibre damage and disturbance of mechanical forces. Elastic fibres, that is elastin and fibrillin, maintain the integrity of the alveolar septa and ensure mechanical recoil on expiration. Proteases, that is neutrophil elastase, MMP-12 and cathepsins, break down elastin. Oxidants, for their part, inactivate alpha-1 antitrypsin, A1AT, and oxidise elastin. Elastic fibre damage is not the primary cause but a consequence. However, it plays a harmful part in the onset and progression of disease. As a result the air spaces enlarge. If stretch and recoil are disturbed, uneven damage gives zones of stress and compensatory over-distension of the remaining alveoli. The damage continues.

t: Order of relative importance of the mechanisms
n: Let us remember the order of relative importance of the mechanisms. In first place is the protease–antiprotease imbalance. It is the central one, in genetic and smoking-related emphysema. Second is oxidative stress: it enhances protease and increases apoptosis. Third is chronic inflammation, the source of proteases and oxidants. In fourth and fifth place are apoptosis and disturbance of repair and traction; they are mainly a consequence, not a cause. Attention: do not make the mistake of regarding apoptosis and disturbed repair as initiators.

t: Case analysis: a smoker and alpha-1 antitrypsin
n: Case analysis. Situation: a smoker under 45 has breathlessness and chronic cough with sputum, and emphysema has been found. Alpha-1 antitrypsin is the main inhibitor of neutrophil elastase. In deficiency the risk rises, especially in smokers. Smoking increases oxidants. Oxidants inactivate protease inhibitors and intensify tissue destruction. The question is as follows: which mechanisms act together in this patient, and why should alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency be checked? Think about the answer on the basis of the mechanisms described.

We consolidate the pathogenesis of emphysema with quick questions. Question 1: which hypothesis of pathogenesis is regarded as the central one in genetic and smoking-related emphysema? Question 2: is damage to elastic fibres the initial cause of emphysema or a consequence? What is its final result? Question 3: by which two routes are elastin fibres broken down? Give examples. Question 4: inflammation associated with which lymphocytes continues even after smoking cessation? Find the answers in the mechanisms of the previous slides.

t: Small airways: definition and the "silent zone"
n: Now we turn to the small airways. They are bronchioles without cartilaginous support, with an internal diameter of less than 2 mm. In COPD they are heavily affected at the earliest stage. They consist of membranous and respiratory bronchioles and alveolar ducts, beginning at about the 8th–15th generation of branching and ending with the terminal bronchioles. The lumen is narrow and there is no cartilaginous support, so they are extremely sensitive to harmful particles. But they are clinically silent, which is why they are called the silent zone. Impairment of small airway function often begins before symptoms or changes on spirometry or X-ray appear. The terminal bronchioles may disappear first.

We compare the small and large airways. The wall of the small airways is thin, lined by ciliated columnar epithelium and, distally, cuboidal epithelium. In the normal state they contribute about 10% of the total resistance, whereas at an early stage of COPD the resistance rises markedly. In the small airways gas flow is mainly laminar, the Reynolds number is low, and the effect of gas density is small or absent. The surfactant layer prevents collapse. In the large airways the flow is mainly turbulent, and the effect of gas density is marked. At the end of expiration the tethering force decreases, and the small airways are prone to collapse.

t: Small airway disease: a three-stage path
n: Small airway disease proceeds in three stages. Initiation: tobacco smoke and pollution damage the epithelium, forming a mucus plug. Expansion: neutrophils enter, then macrophages and T lymphocytes, and mediators and cell senescence intensify. Remodelling: smooth muscle hyperplasia, fibrosis and loss of capillaries narrow the airways. That is, the process begins with epithelial damage and ends with permanent structural change.

Initiation stage: epithelial injury and EMT. Smoke and air pollution damage the epithelium of the small airways again and again, and the cycle of injury and repair repeats. The TGF-β, Wnt/β-catenin and Notch pathways trigger epithelial-mesenchymal transition, that is EMT. The cell acquires the properties of mesenchyme. STAT3 enhances fibrosis. If PINK1-Parkin is impaired, reactive oxygen species, ROS, increase. The chain is as follows: smoke exposure, epithelial injury and repair, EMT with fibrosis and remodelling, then barrier disruption and plug.

Mucus plug and barrier disruption. Smoke and pollution lead to an increase in goblet cells and a rise in the mucin proteins MUC5AC and MUC5B. Tight junction proteins are disrupted, and mucociliary clearance and barrier integrity deteriorate. Secretory IgA, SIgA, and the polymeric immunoglobulin receptor, pIgR, decrease. The antimicrobial barrier weakens, and susceptibility to infection rises. Accumulation of mucus obstructs airflow and creates a favourable environment for microbial growth. The plug is related to disease severity.

t: Case analysis: mucus plug in the small airways
n: Case analysis. Situation: a smoker has normal spirometry. According to the source, even in patients with pathological changes FEV1 and FVC may be preserved. Analysis: the small airways may start the disease early with epithelial injury, plugging and inflammation, but spirometry may not detect it. Question: if spirometry is normal, which methods can detect small airway injury early? Attention: normal spirometry does not mean healthy small airways. The frequency of plugs is related to disease severity.

In the expansion stage, immune cells and mediators are engaged. Cigarette smoke and particles activate the epithelium and alveolar macrophages. They release TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6 and CXCL8, LTB4, that is chemokines. In COPD neutrophils are the first to enter the small airways. Then macrophages and CD4+/CD8+ T lymphocytes come, damaging the tissue cytotoxically. Smoke and particles, by activating the NF-κB and p38 MAPK pathways, continue the release of cytokines. Oxidative stress also triggers PI3K/Akt/mTOR. Attention: in about 20–40 per cent of patients with COPD there is an eosinophilic phenotype. It is associated with small airway dysfunction and may respond well to inhaled corticosteroids.

Cell senescence and SASP. Inflammation and oxidative stress drive cells into a state of senescence via the ATM/ATR–p53/p21 pathway. Senescent cells release SASP, that is the secretory phenotype: IL-6, IL-8, MMP-9 and MMP-12. Neighbouring cells also senesce, and thus a loop of secondary senescence forms. miR-34a rises and weakens SIRT1/6, that is antioxidant and repair enzymes. As a result SASP becomes persistent.

The NLRP3 inflammasome and substance P. The NLRP3 inflammasome is an amplifier of inflammation: ROS, extracellular ATP and lysosomal instability activate it, and IL-1β and IL-18 mature. IL-1β recruits neutrophils and forms a ROS–IL-1β amplification loop. In experiment, blocking NLRP3 broke this loop. Substance P gives neurogenic inflammation in response to smoke exposure: mucus release and infiltration are intensified. Its excessive expression may lead to fibrosis. NK1 receptor antagonists, for example aprepitant, reduced inflammation and fibrosis in an animal model. The mechanism and clinical evidence are at an initial stage.

In the remodelling stage, smooth muscle and fibrosis change. Smooth muscle cells multiply and enlarge, thickening the wall and narrowing the small airways. Fibroblasts become α-SMA-positive myofibroblasts and produce much type I/III collagen and laminin. The MMP/TIMP balance is disturbed, and matrix breakdown and collagen deposition proceed simultaneously. The chain: injury and inflammation, release of TGF-β and PDGF, muscle proliferation and EMT, collagen I/III in the myofibroblast, and finally stiffening of the wall and irreversible narrowing.

Vascular changes are of two types: arterial and capillary. Arterial remodelling and capillary rarefaction are two separate angiopathies with different effects. In arterial change the intima thickens, the lumen narrows, vascular resistance rises, and hypertension and right ventricular dysfunction appear. In capillary change, capillary density decreases, diffusing capacity, DLCO, falls, and hypoxaemia and V/Q mismatch are seen. On tomography, reduction in the volume of distal arteries, that is arterial pruning, predicts acceleration of emphysema. They are synergistic: arterial hypertension increases capillary loss, and capillary loss increases resistance.

Single-cell omics data. In an atlas of terminal bronchioles in early-stage COPD, GOLD I–II, M1-like macrophages and neutrophils accumulate at the sites where alveoli attach. These cells are associated with breakdown of elastic fibres: immune infiltration and matrix damage are close in time and place. The ligand–receptor network of basal cells, fibroblasts and immune cells regulates inflammatory and matrix factors, intensifying irreversible remodelling. In T cells and macrophages, RNA methylation and autophagy genes are active and linked with inflammation. This epigenetic signal may be an upstream step.

Case analysis: arterial pruning. Situation: in the COPDGene cohort, reduction in the volume of distal small arteries on CT, that is arterial pruning, was studied. It is associated with progression of emphysema. Even without accounting for baseline parenchymal damage, initial arterial pruning predicted acceleration of emphysema and decline in lung function. In smokers without obvious signs of COPD, early arterial pruning may raise pulmonary vascular resistance and contribute to right ventricular remodelling. Question: why is arterial pruning interpreted not only as an accompanying change but as an independent factor in disease progression?

t: Quick question: small airways and remodelling
n: Quick questions on small airways and remodelling. Question 1: during EMT, that is epithelial-mesenchymal transition, what do epithelial cells lose and what phenotype do they acquire? Question 2: what is SASP, that is senescence-associated secretory phenotype, and which factors does it include? Question 3: which three processes in the remodelling stage are linked to each other in time and place? Attention: arterial remodelling and capillary rarefaction are not the same. The first raises vascular resistance, the second lowers diffusing capacity, DLCO.

Early detection begins with spirometry. MMEF, that is FEF25–75%, is the mean forced flow over the 25–75% portion of FVC. It reflects the peripheral airways, falls in early small airway disease, SAD, and is more sensitive than FEV1. But the sensitivity and specificity of MMEF are insufficient. In early SAD, FEV1 and FVC may be preserved, so the sensitivity of spirometry is limited. An alternative index is FEV3/FEV6: FEV3 covers more of the small airway air, and FEV6 removes the need to measure FVC precisely. If FEV3/FEV6 is below the lower limit of normal, then even in smokers with normal FEV1/FVC, air trapping and fSAD, that is functional small airway disease, may be detected on CT.

We compare washout tests and impulse oscillometry. Single-breath washout, SBW, is simple and quick, but requires a maximal breath, cooperation is needed, and sensitivity is limited. Multiple-breath washout, MBW, is performed in quiet breathing and suits children. LCI shows ventilation inhomogeneity, but the test is lengthy and a special gas analyser is needed. Impulse oscillometry, IOS, adds oscillation to quiet breathing. R5–R20 and X5 assess the small airways. IOS requires no effort and is sensitive; its drawback is that it may not agree with other methods.

Frequency dependence of dynamic compliance. Dynamic compliance, Cdyn, reflects together the elasticity of the lung and the resistance of the airways. In a healthy lung the time constant is uniform, so even if breathing quickens Cdyn hardly changes. When the small airways are narrowed, the time constant is uneven, as the respiratory rate increases some regions do not empty, and Cdyn falls. As Woolcock showed, if the usual tests are normal but Cdyn is reduced in rapid breathing, this is a sign of hidden obstruction.

HRCT and parametric response mapping, PRM. HRCT is the most effective method, but its resolution is about 2 mm, so the terminal bronchioles are not visible. PRM, using paired scans, separates functional small airway disease, fSAD, from emphysema. Steps: inspiratory and expiratory scan, registration of the scans, analysis of each voxel by HU value, separation of fSAD or emphysema and obtaining the result as a 3D map. Limitation: two scans, high radiation and cost. For the bronchial wall and mucus plug, HRCT is needed.

We compare SPECT and 19F MRI. Single-photon emission tomography, SPECT, assesses ventilation inhomogeneity by AUC-CV. It uses an inhaled radioactive tracer, detects even mild changes, and is mainly a research tool. In 19F magnetic resonance imaging, MRI, VDP shows local air trapping, whereas FEV1, that is the volume in the 1st second, shows overall limitation. It works with the inert gas perfluoropropane, is simple, economical and safe, but is not widely available and requires breath-holding. Both methods are mainly research tools and are not yet included in the everyday diagnosis of COPD.

A final comparison of diagnostic methods. Spirometry is simple and cheap, the most widely used, but in early small airway disease, SAD, its sensitivity is insufficient. Multiple-breath washout, MBW, and impulse oscillometry, IOS, are more sensitive even when spirometry is normal. MBW suits children, and IOS requires little effort. Parametric response mapping, PRM, separates fSAD from emphysema, but requires two scans, is expensive and involves radiation. SPECT and 19F MRI detect regional ventilation, but they are research tools and little available.

t: Experimental models and biomarkers of emphysema
n: Experimental models and biomarkers of emphysema. Animal models reflect some features of human disease, and the mouse is used most. In the smoking model, inflammation and alveolar rupture occur, and smoke dose and species differences have an effect. In the elastase model, elastic fibres are broken down, it develops quickly, whereas in humans it is chronic. In the chemical model ozone, nitrogen and sulphur dioxide are used, and dose and duration do not correspond to real life. In genetically modified models — increased MMP-12, absence of elastase or A1AT — it is hard to control the effect of age and sex. As for biomarkers, sRAGE in the blood is related to disease severity. Desmosine is an amino acid specific to elastin, a sensitive and specific marker of destruction of the alveolar wall.

Bronchodilators relax the muscles of the airways, reducing the fall in airflow and the difficulty of breathing. They are of two groups: β-2 agonists and anticholinergics. β-2 agonists stimulate β-2 adrenoceptors: adenylate cyclase, cAMP, protein kinase A. Smooth muscle relaxes and the airways widen. Short-acting salbutamol is for quick relief. Long-acting LABAs, salmeterol and formoterol, are for continuous treatment. Indacaterol is used once a day. Anticholinergics block M3 muscarinic receptors. Ipratropium bromide is short-acting, while long-acting LAMAs are the mainstay of treatment. Glycopyrronium and aclidinium bromide are also in this group.

Corticosteroids, antibiotics and PDE4 inhibitors. Corticosteroids bind to the glucocorticoid receptor and weaken NF-κB and AP-1. They are given mainly to patients with frequent exacerbations, most often by inhalation. Risks: infection, weight gain, hypertension, osteoporosis, sometimes corticosteroid resistance. Antibiotics do not treat emphysema, since the disease is not caused by infection, but in a bacterial exacerbation recovery is faster. Macrolides are anti-inflammatory in vitro. PDE4 inhibitors act in neutrophils, T cells and macrophages: roflumilast, rolipram, cilomilast. Adverse effects: nausea, diarrhoea, headache, insomnia. Ensifentrine is a PDE3/PDE4 inhibitor.

t: Treatment and management: approaches in emphysema
n: The approaches to treatment and management are stepwise. In the GOLD guidance, that is the Global Initiative for COPD, smoking cessation is the first-line measure that slows progression of the disease. First, risk factors: stopping smoking, avoiding pollution. For urgent relief, a short-acting bronchodilator. As the disease progresses, a long-acting bronchodilator. Long-acting anticholinergics and β-2 agonists, LAMA/LABA, with or without a corticosteroid, reduce symptoms. In frequent exacerbations or severe symptoms a corticosteroid is added. In severe emphysema lung volume reduction is considered, and in the terminal stage, lung transplantation.

t: New directions: antifibrotic and senolytic therapy
n: New directions: antifibrotic and senolytic therapy. Inhaled glucocorticoids, ICS, suppress inflammatory genes. If eosinophils in the blood are many, the effect is better. Pirfenidone acts on the transforming growth factor-β, TGF-β, pathway, and nintedanib, that is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor, weakens fibroblast proliferation. Dasatinib with quercetin removes senescent cells and in a mouse model of pulmonary fibrosis reduced fibrotic factors; in humans the evidence is still scant. The future: senolytics, interventions based on microRNA or exosomes, anti-TGF-β and antioxidant therapy, and targeting neutrophils and the PI3Kδ pathway.

Conclusion: key messages. There are three interrelated mechanisms: chronic inflammation, fibrosis and epithelial-mesenchymal transition, EMT, and cell senescence and its secretory phenotype, SASP. Emphysema is the main component of COPD, characterised by destruction of the alveolar walls and loss of lung elasticity. Small airway disease, SAD, may begin before alveolar destruction, and so is important in the early stage of COPD. Principle: early detection, early diagnosis, early treatment. When spirometry is normal, MBW, that is multiple-breath washout, and IOS, that is impulse oscillometry, are more sensitive.
